passage:
Supervisor's note, final-year project office.
Jahnavi asked if she could make one phone call from my office before our meeting, and whether I would stay. She had decided to take the rural health fellowship instead of the corporate offer her parents had been proud of. She put the phone on the table and spoke slowly. "Papa, Ma, I know you want the best for me, and I'm grateful for everything. I've chosen the fellowship. I'd really like your blessing, but I'll take responsibility for it either way." There was a long silence. Then her father said, "Send us the details. We'll read them." Jahnavi let out her breath.
I told her I thought she had spoken with both kindness and spine, and we went on to her chapter two.
— Rafiq, project supervisor

qa.q: What offer did Jahnavi turn down?
qa.a: She turned down the corporate offer her parents had been proud of.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi letting out her breath suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had been nervous and tense and felt relieved when her father asked for the details instead of arguing.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi's way of speaking work?
qa.a: She combined thanks for her parents' care with a clear, calm decision and took responsibility, so they could hear her without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's father have received her words?
qa.a: He may have felt respected even while disappointed, which is why he asked to read the details rather than refusing outright.

grounding: It shows a young woman telling her parents with gratitude and firmness that she has chosen her path, wanting their blessing but accepting responsibility.

passage:
Sunday night
I did it. After lunch, when Mummy and Papa were having tea, I sat across from them. My knees were shaking under the table.
I said, "I know you want the best for me, and I'm really grateful. I want to marry Vaibhav. I've thought about it for two years. I would love your blessing, but either way, this is my choice and I'll take responsibility for it."
Papa didn't say anything for ages. Mummy's eyes filled up. Then Papa said, "Bring him home for dinner next week. We want to meet him properly."
I didn't expect that. I cried in the bathroom after, happy crying. 🙏
Still a long way to go. But they heard me.
Yamini

qa.q: When did Papa ask Yamini to bring Vaibhav home?
qa.a: Papa asked her to bring Vaibhav home for dinner next week.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling while she spoke to her parents?
qa.a: She was very nervous, with shaking knees, but also determined, and afterwards relieved and happy.

qa.q: What made Yamini's talk likely to be heard?
qa.a: She thanked her parents and acknowledged their care, then stated her choice calmly and owned it, without blaming or demanding.

qa.q: How might Yamini's mother be feeling with her eyes filling up?
qa.a: She may feel a mix of worry, sadness at letting go and being moved by how respectfully her daughter spoke.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman stating her choice of partner with gratitude and firmness, asking for her parents' blessing while taking responsibility.

passage: The power in Aizawl had been out since noon, so Lalremsiami sat by the window with her phone at nine percent, calling her mother. "Nu, I have to choose by tonight. The Delhi job pays more, but the Shillong one is the work I love." Her flatmate Damini lit a candle between them. A year ago, her mother would have decided for her in one sentence. Now there was a pause. "If it were me, I'd think about the cost of living in Delhi. But you know your life better now. Whatever you choose, and even if it doesn't work out, you can always call me." Siami blinked. The phone died. Damini grinned. "So? What did she say?" "She said it's my choice."

qa.q: How much battery did Siami's phone have when she called?
qa.a: Her phone was at nine percent.

qa.q: How can you tell Siami felt surprised by her mother's answer?
qa.a: She blinked, because a year ago her mother would have decided for her, and now she only gave advice.

qa.q: What makes the mother's new approach helpful?
qa.a: She shares one practical thought but leaves the decision to Siami and accepts she might make a mistake, which treats her as an adult.

qa.q: How might Siami's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: She may feel a little anxious but also proud that her daughter is making her own decisions.

grounding: It shows a parent shifting from deciding to advising, accepting that her adult daughter may err, as a relationship of two adults grows.

passage: The little shop on Linking Road in Mumbai smelled of fresh paint. Zeenat's father stood in the doorway, turning a tote bag over in his hands. Two years ago he had told her the handmade bag business was a waste of her commerce degree. Now he just asked, "Your supplier from Surat, is the contract clear on returns?" "Mostly," Zeenat said. "Show a lawyer friend before you sign. But your decision." Her partner Tanuja raised her eyebrows at Zeenat behind his back. When the first customer bought two bags, he stepped aside and let Zeenat handle the counter. Later, at home, Zeenat heard him on the phone to her uncle: "My daughter runs her own shop now, you know."

qa.q: What did Zeenat's father ask about the Surat supplier?
qa.a: He asked whether the contract was clear on returns.

qa.q: What does her father's phone call to her uncle show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows he feels proud of Zeenat and her independence, even though he once called the business a waste.

qa.q: What changed in the way Zeenat's father helps her?
qa.a: He moved from deciding for her to giving advice and letting her choose, even stepping aside at the counter.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Zeenat's father?
qa.a: She seems surprised and amused, raising her eyebrows at how differently he behaves now. 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a parent moving from decision-maker to advisor and taking pride in the young adult's independence.

subtype: Stage 1: A new claim on attention [Actor]
passage:

Chirag (5) was building with blocks when his mother, Lavanya, arrived carrying baby Lakshay with a shiny new rattle. Chirag ran to her, then saw the baby on her hip. He stopped. He grabbed the rattle and hit Lakshay's hand with it. Lakshay cried. Chirag's lip shook.
I knelt beside him. "You wanted Mumma's lap too." He nodded and pressed his face into my shoulder.
I suggested Lavanya give Chirag a hug first at pickup tomorrow. 🙂
— Charu Miss

qa.q: What was baby Lakshay holding?
qa.a: Lakshay was holding a shiny new rattle.

qa.q: What was Chirag feeling when he saw the baby on his mother's hip?
qa.a: He felt left out and hurt, even though he loves his mother and brother, and he could not say it in words.

qa.a: Charu Miss suggested Lavanya hug Chirag first at pickup, so he feels he still has his place.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel seeing Chirag hit the baby?
qa.a: She may feel upset and confused, not realising at first that Chirag is feeling pushed aside.

subtype: Stage 1: A new claim on attention [Actor]

Zubin stood by the door. Then he marched over, grabbed the top and pushed Kaizad's arm. Kaizad wailed. "Zubin!" Mamma said. Zubin threw the top on the floor and ran behind the cupboard. Ritu Masi found him there, hugging his knees. She sat down beside him and opened her arms.

passage:
Play centre note, Saturday morning.
Samir (5) and his sister Sofia (3) were at the block corner. Their father sat nearby on his phone. Sofia built a tall tower. Samir watched her, then watched his father. He swept the tower over with one hand. Then he looked straight at his father. His father looked up and said, "Samir, why?" Samir shrugged. He didn't know.
I asked Samir to help me build a bigger tower with Sofia. He did.
— Francis, play centre staff

qa.q: Who built the tall tower?
qa.a: Sofia built the tall tower.

qa.q: What did Samir want when he looked straight at his father?

qa.q: What could Samir's father try next time?
qa.a: He could put the phone away and notice Samir before trouble starts, like playing blocks with both children.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel when her tower falls?
qa.a: She probably feels upset and confused, since she was only building and her brother knocked it over. 😢

grounding: It shows a boy knocking over his sister's blocks and watching to see if a parent looks at him, not knowing himself why he did it.

passage: In the mud courtyard of their house, Tanvir's sister Damini was stacking small clay pots into a tower. Amma sat nearby, sorting rice. Tanvir, five, sat on the step, watching Amma, who did not look up. He walked over and kicked the tower. The pots rolled everywhere. Damini shrieked. Tanvir looked at Amma. Now Amma looked. "Tanvir! What did you do that for?" Tanvir stood there, scratching his leg. He did not know what to say. He just looked at Amma.

qa.q: What was Damini stacking into a tower?
qa.a: She was stacking small clay pots into a tower.

qa.a: He wanted Amma to look at him, because she had been busy and not noticing him.

grounding: It illustrates a boy knocking over his sister's tower and watching whether his mother will look, where even a scolding is attention.

passage:
"Mummaaa! Divyansh broke my doll's house!"
"She hit me first!"
"No! You broke it first! So I hit you!"
Binita's face was red and wet. She pushed Divyansh again.
"Ow! Mumma, she pushed me!"
"Because you're mean!"
"You're meaner!"
Mumma came in with a towel over her shoulder. "Stop, both of you. What happened?"
"HE started it!"
"SHE hit first!"
Binita stamped her foot and screamed. Divyansh started crying too. Both of them pointed at each other.

passage:
Note from Harish Dada, for Beta and Bahu.
Ovi (4) and Ojas (6) were playing with the train set this afternoon. Ojas took the engine. Ovi screamed and hit his arm. Ojas pushed her down. Then both cried.
Ovi: "He took my engine!"
Ojas: "She hit me first!"

subtype: Stage 4: Parent takes sides by accident [Observer]
passage: In the clinic waiting room, Elizabeth, the nurse, was filling a form when she heard a crash. Six-year-old Anjali and her little brother Mihir had pulled at the same picture book. Mihir fell and started howling. Their father jumped up, scooped Mihir into his arms and turned to Anjali. "You're older! Be sensible!" Anjali's arms dropped. "But he..." "No buts." Anjali sat back on her chair alone, swinging her legs hard. Elizabeth saw her wipe her eyes with her sleeve and stare at the floor.

qa.q: What were Anjali and Mihir pulling at?
qa.a: They were pulling at the same picture book.

qa.a: She felt blamed and unheard, and sad that her father took Mihir's side without listening.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Anjali after the scolding?
qa.a: Elizabeth notices a hurt little girl sitting alone, wiping her eyes and staring at the floor.

passage: I'm Maria, and I live next door to Simran's family. Yesterday I heard a scream. Simran, who is five, and her baby brother were both holding the same ball. The baby started crying. Their mother came running. She picked up the baby and said, "Simran, you're the big sister! Why can't you just give it?" Simran said, "But it's mine!" Her mother said, "You're older, be sensible." Simran went quiet and sat in the corner of the balcony. I don't know what she was thinking. But this is the third time this week I've heard the same words.

qa.a: They were both holding the same ball.

qa.a: Maria notices that the same words, "You're older, be sensible," have been said three times this week, which worries Maria. 😔

grounding: It illustrates a parent comforting the crying younger child and scolding the older one with you're older, be sensible, a repeated pattern.

subtype: Stage 5: Separate, calm, listen to both [Response]
passage:
Mother's journal, Wednesday.
Ayaan (6) and Mehr (4) fought over the block tower again. Mehr knocked it down; Ayaan pushed her. Both screamed.
This time I didn't shout. I took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug, then sat on the floor between them. I asked Ayaan first. "You wanted your tower." He nodded, tears falling. Then Mehr. "You felt scared when he pushed you." She nodded too.
In two minutes both were calm. 🤍 Ayaan offered to build another one.
— Salma

qa.q: Where did Salma take Ayaan and Mehr?
qa.a: She took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug.

qa.q: How can you tell Ayaan felt understood?
qa.a: He nodded with tears falling when Salma said he wanted his tower, and later offered to build another one.

qa.q: Why did Salma's approach calm the fight so quickly?
qa.a: She separated them, sat at their level and named each child's feeling, so both felt heard instead of judged.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehr when Salma names her fear?
qa.a: Mehr likely feels safe and understood, which is why she nods and calms down.

grounding: It shows a parent separating the children, getting down to their level, letting each speak and naming their feelings, which cools the fight.

passage:
Raghav, you think your mother never felt jealous of me? Let me tell you. When your Amma was ten and I was twelve, all the relatives came for Diwali. Every aunty patted my head: "Hemant got ninety-five in maths! Such a bright boy!" Nobody asked about Sunanda's drawings, which were better than anything I did. I saw her go quiet. That night she didn't want to eat sweets. She told me, "They love you more." I laughed, stupidly. After that she stopped playing carrom with me. Every good mark I got felt like it took something from her. We only became friends again when we were grown. They didn't mean harm, but comparing us made us rivals.
— Hemant Mama

qa.q: What marks did Hemant get in maths?
qa.a: He got ninety-five in maths.

qa.q: What was Sunanda feeling when she said, "They love you more"?
qa.a: She felt less loved and overlooked, because the relatives only praised her brother's marks and ignored her drawings.

qa.q: What could the relatives or parents have done differently at this first stage?
qa.a: They could have praised each child for their own strengths, like Sunanda's drawings, instead of comparing, so neither felt they had to compete.

qa.q: How does Hemant Mama see that time now?
qa.a: He regrets laughing and sees that the comparison, though not meant to hurt, turned his sister into a rival.

grounding: It shows a ten-year-old girl hearing relatives praise her brother's marks and starting to feel less loved, as comparison turns siblings into rivals.

passage: The wedding hall was loud, and the lights kept flickering because of the generator. Gargi, ten, was carrying a plate of laddoos for her grandmother when she heard Neelam Bua in the crowd. "Neel came first in his class again! Such a clever boy. Gargi is... well, she's good at dancing." Everyone laughed and turned to look at Neel. Gargi's plate wobbled. Then the lights went off. qa.a: She carried a plate of laddoos for her grandmother.

passage: In the village near Tumkur, Amma cut the ripe mango into pieces on a steel plate. Shankar, eleven, leaned close. "Lokesh got the big piece with the seed!" Lokesh, nine, grabbed it. "You got two pieces yesterday!" "And you slept later on Sunday!" "You got new chappals first!" Amma put down the knife. The boys were not looking at the mango anymore; they were looking at her, waiting to see whose side she would take. Shankar's voice cracked a little. "You always give him more." Amma looked at the two of them, their faces fierce, and understood it wasn't really about mango at all.

qa.a: She was cutting the ripe mango into pieces.

qa.a: It suggests he wants to know he matters to Amma as much as Lokesh does, not just a bigger piece of mango.

qa.q: What could Amma do at this turning point?
qa.a: Instead of weighing pieces, she could reassure each boy of her love and give each some time alone with her, which answers the real need.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see the mango fight?
qa.a: Lokesh probably feels he is the one treated unfairly, remembering Shankar's two pieces yesterday.

grounding: It shows two children keeping count of shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact equality, when underneath they need to know they matter equally.

passage: In their Melbourne flat, Valentina, eleven, stood at the fridge with a notebook. "Mei got a new phone case and I didn't. That's three things this month." Mei, nine, ran in. "You stayed up till nine-thirty on Friday! I had to sleep at nine!" "Because I'm older!" "You got the bigger slice of pizza!" Their father looked up from the stove. "Are you two keeping score?" Valentina held up her notebook proudly. It had columns: Mei, Me. He sat down at the table. "What would it mean if Mei got more?" Valentina's face changed. She said quietly, "That you like her more." Mei looked at her sister, surprised. "I thought you thought that about me."

qa.q: What columns did Valentina's notebook have?
qa.a: It had two columns: Mei and Me.

qa.q: What does Valentina's quiet answer reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: It reveals she is worried her father likes Mei more, so keeping score is really about feeling she matters.

qa.q: Why was the father's question a good turning point?
qa.a: Asking what it would mean if Mei got more helped Valentina say the real worry, so he can reassure both girls rather than count things.

qa.q: What does Mei's reply show about how she sees things?
qa.a: It shows Mei had the same fear, thinking she was the one who mattered less.

grounding: It illustrates siblings counting shares, bedtimes and new things and demanding exact fairness, when underneath each needs to know they matter as much.
